A boulder is a very large, naturally occurring rock. It is so large that a single person cannot lift it, and it typically requires heavy machinery (like a crane or bulldozer) to move it. Think of it as a rock that dominates its surroundings just by sitting there.

Boulders are usually rounded or somewhat smooth on the outside. This is because over thousands or millions of years, forces like flowing water, glaciers, and wind gradually wear down the sharp edges of a rock, giving it a rounder, smoother shape. However, a boulder doesn't have to be perfectly round — some are jagged, irregular, or flat-sided, especially if they broke off a cliff recently and haven't had time to be smoothed out yet.

In terms of color and texture, boulders look exactly like the type of rock they are made of — they can be grey granite, reddish sandstone, dark basalt, and so on. The word "boulder" tells you about the size of the rock, not what it is made of.

In everyday language, people use "boulder" loosely to mean any rock that is too big to pick up — roughly the size of a basketball or larger. But in geology (the science of rocks and the Earth), the word has a precise, agreed-upon meaning.

Geologists use a measurement system called the Wentworth scale to classify loose rock and sediment by size. According to this scale:

  • A boulder is any rock with a diameter (width) of more than 256 millimeters — that is roughly 25.6 centimeters, or just over 10 inches.

So if a rock is smaller than that, geologists would call it a cobble (64–256 mm) or a pebble (4–64 mm), not a boulder.

In practice, though, when people picture a "boulder," they usually imagine something much larger than 256 mm — more like something the size of a car, a small house, or even bigger. All of those still count as boulders. The 256 mm threshold is simply the minimum size at which a rock earns the name.

Boulders don't appear out of nowhere. They come from larger bodies of rock that break apart over time. Here are the main ways this happens:

1. Weathering and Erosion
Rock faces on mountains, cliffs, and hillsides are constantly exposed to rain, wind, freezing temperatures, and the roots of plants. Over time, these forces crack and chip away at the rock. Large chunks eventually break off and tumble down — and those chunks are boulders.

2. Glaciers
During ice ages, enormous slow-moving rivers of ice called glaciers scraped across the land and picked up massive rocks embedded in the ground. As glaciers moved, they carried these rocks — sometimes hundreds of kilometers — before melting and dropping them far from where they started. A boulder left behind this way is called a glacial erratic. This is why you sometimes find a huge, lone boulder sitting in the middle of flat farmland with no obvious explanation — a glacier left it there thousands of years ago.

3. Rockfalls and Landslides
When part of a cliff or steep hillside collapses suddenly, the falling chunks of rock become boulders. These often pile up at the base of the cliff, forming what is called a talus slope — a sloping heap of loose rock fragments, including boulders.

4. River and Ocean Activity
Rivers carry rocks downstream. Over a very long time, these rocks knock against each other and against the riverbed, chipping away at each other's sharp edges. This is how boulders get their characteristic rounded shape. Ocean waves do the same thing along coastlines.

Boulders can be found almost anywhere on Earth:

  • Riverbeds and riverbanks — partly or fully submerged, smoothed by water
  • Beaches and coastlines — worn smooth by waves
  • Mountain slopes and valley floors — from rockfalls and glacial activity
  • Open plains and fields — left behind by ancient glaciers
  • Deserts — shaped by wind erosion over millions of years
  • Forests — often covered in moss and partially buried in soil

Since English has many words for rocks, here is how "boulder" fits into the picture:

  • Rock / Stone: These are general words that can refer to any piece of mineral material, of any size — from a tiny chip to a mountain. A boulder is a rock, but not every rock is a boulder.
  • Pebble: A small, smooth rock — the kind you can easily hold in your palm or throw across water. Far too small to be a boulder.
  • Cobble / Cobblestone: Bigger than a pebble but smaller than a boulder. About the size of a fist. Cobblestones are the rounded stones used to pave old streets.
  • Boulder: Larger than a cobble. Too heavy and big to lift by hand.
  • Bedrock: The solid layer of rock that sits underneath the soil. Unlike a boulder, bedrock is not a loose, separate rock — it is connected to the Earth beneath your feet and cannot simply be picked up or rolled away.

The size order, from smallest to largest, goes roughly: pebble → cobble → boulder.

Outside of its literal meaning, people sometimes use "boulder" in casual speech to just emphasize that something is very large and heavy. For example, someone might exaggerate and say "that bag weighs as much as a boulder" to mean it is extremely heavy. This is a figurative (non-literal) use — it paints a picture rather than making a scientific claim.

A boulder is a large, naturally occurring rock — geologically defined as any loose rock wider than 256 millimeters, though in everyday use the word suggests something much larger, often too big for a person or even a small group of people to move without machinery. Boulders are formed when large bodies of rock break apart through weathering, glacial movement, rockfalls, or water erosion. They are found all over the world, in rivers, on mountains, on beaches, and in open fields. The word tells you about size, not about what the rock is made of.
